title_en: Marie Curie: Light from the Shed
description_ru: Жизнь первой женщины, получившей две Нобелевские премии в разных науках: от варшавского подполья до радия и фронтовых рентгеновских машин.
text:
On a cold morning in 1891, a twenty-four-year-old Polish woman stepped off a train in Paris carrying a modest trunk, a folding chair and almost no money. She had spent years saving for this journey, and she had no intention of wasting it. Her name was Maria Skłodowska, and within four decades she would become the only person in history to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

She was born in Warsaw in 1867, at a time when Poland did not exist as an independent state. The city belonged to the Russian Empire, which forbade lessons in Polish history and discouraged ambitious girls from setting foot in a university. Her parents were teachers, proud of their culture and chronically short of money, and when her mother died of tuberculosis and her eldest sister of typhus, the household grew grim. Maria nevertheless finished school at fifteen with a gold medal. Because women were not admitted to the University of Warsaw, she joined the so-called Flying University, a clandestine network whose classes met in private apartments and moved whenever the police grew suspicious.

The bargain she made with her sister Bronisława was typical of her determination. Maria would work as a governess and pay for Bronisława's medical studies in Paris, and in return Bronisława would later support her. It took six years. When Maria finally reached the Sorbonne, she enrolled under the French version of her name, Marie, rented a freezing attic and frequently forgot to eat. On one occasion she fainted in a lecture hall from hunger. Yet she graduated first in physics in 1893 and second in mathematics the following year.

It was a search for laboratory space that led her to Pierre Curie, a reserved physicist already respected for his work on magnetism and crystals. They fell in love through long conversations about science, and in 1895 they married in a simple civil ceremony. She wore a dark blue suit that she afterwards used as a working outfit, and the couple spent their honeymoon cycling through the French countryside.

The following year, Henri Becquerel reported that uranium salts gave off mysterious rays, and Marie chose them as the subject of her doctoral research. Using a delicate electrometer built by Pierre and his brother Jacques, she made a decisive observation: the strength of the rays depended only on the amount of uranium present, not on its chemical form. The radiation, she concluded, must come from the atom itself, a daring idea at a time when atoms were thought to be indivisible. She coined the word "radioactivity". She also noticed that pitchblende, the ore from which uranium is extracted, was far more active than its uranium content could explain, and she reasoned that it must conceal something new.

Pierre set aside his own research to join her. In 1898 they announced the discovery of two elements, polonium, named in honour of her occupied homeland, and radium. But announcing an element and proving that it exists are different matters, because chemists demand a visible sample. For four years, in a leaky former dissecting room with an earth floor, the Curies processed tonnes of pitchblende residue, shipped from a mine in Bohemia, stirring boiling cauldrons with iron rods nearly as tall as she was. By 1902 she had isolated a tenth of a gram of pure radium chloride. Looking back, she called those years the happiest of their lives.

Recognition arrived swiftly. In 1903 the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded jointly to Becquerel and to the Curies, though the committee had originally intended to honour only the men; Pierre insisted that his wife's name be included, and a sympathetic member of the Swedish Academy helped to ensure it. The fame that followed was unwelcome. Journalists camped outside their door, manufacturers sold radium-flavoured cosmetics, and the couple, exhausted and often unwell, longed for the shed.

Then, in April 1906, Pierre stepped into a rain-slicked Paris street and was killed by a horse-drawn wagon. Marie was thirty-eight, with two young daughters and a grief she described in her diary as almost physical. The Sorbonne offered her Pierre's professorship, and she became the first woman ever to teach there. Her first lecture began exactly at the sentence where his last had ended.

She endured, and her work deepened. In 1910 she isolated metallic radium, but the following year brought a vicious press campaign over her friendship with a married physicist, Paul Langevin. Newspapers called her a foreign homewrecker, and the Academy of Sciences rejected her candidacy by two votes. A member of the Nobel committee even suggested that she should stay away from Stockholm. She went anyway and received the 1911 Prize in Chemistry on her own, an honour no one has matched in two separate scientific fields.

When war broke out in 1914, she saw at once that X-rays could save lives at the front. She persuaded wealthy donors to fund about twenty mobile radiological vehicles, nicknamed "little Curies", learned to drive one herself, and trained dozens of women to operate the equipment. Her teenage daughter Irène worked beside her. Together they helped examine over a million wounded soldiers, enabling surgeons to find bullets and shrapnel instead of probing blindly.

The price was high. For decades Marie carried test tubes in her pockets and kept glowing samples in her desk drawer, admiring their faint blue light in the dark. Her fingertips were scarred and cracked. She died in July 1934 of aplastic anaemia, almost certainly caused by radiation, and her notebooks are still so radioactive that they are stored in lead-lined boxes; visitors to the archive must sign a waiver.

Yet her legacy is not merely a story of sacrifice. She refused to patent the method of extracting radium, insisting that it belonged to science, and she founded institutes that pioneered cancer treatment. Her daughter Irène and son-in-law Frédéric won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1935. In 1995 Marie's remains were moved to the Panthéon in Paris, making her the first woman to be buried there for her own achievements. The immigrant who arrived with a folding chair had rearranged the foundations of physics.

questions.question: Why did Maria Skłodowska go to Paris?
What did the Curies do for four years in the shed?
questions.answer: They processed tonnes of pitchblende to isolate radium.

questions.question: How did Marie Curie help during the First World War?
questions.answer: She organised mobile X-ray vehicles for wounded soldiers.

questions.question: Why was she buried in the Panthéon in 1995?
questions.answer: For her own achievements; she was the first woman buried there on merit.
